analysis.one_liner: Gives patients in managed care plans guaranteed emergency coverage, direct specialist access, outside appeals, and the right to sue their plan.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 196 cosponsors — nearly half the House, including 10 Republicans — but sat in three House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 1998 would have written a set of minimum protections into every group health plan and health insurance policy in the country. Patients would be guaranteed coverage of emergency room care without prior approval, direct access to their OB-GYN and to specialists, standing referrals for chronic illness, coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials, an outside appeal when a plan denies care, and the right to sue the plan in state court for injuries caused by denied care. It died in committee without a single hearing vote or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 160 million Americans then covered by employer-sponsored or other private health insurance, most of it managed care. Someone having a heart attack could go to any emergency room without calling their plan first; a woman could see her gynecologist without a gatekeeper referral; a patient with cancer could get standing referrals to an oncologist, coverage of routine costs in a clinical trial, and exceptions to drug formulary limits when a doctor says an off-list drug is needed. Anyone denied care would get a timely internal appeal and, when health or a large sum of money was on the line, a binding outside appeal paid for by the plan. And unlike then-current law, patients injured by a plan's decision to deny or delay care could sue the plan in state court for damages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People enrolled in managed care and HMO plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to cover emergency services under the prudent layperson standard — no prior authorization, at out-of-network emergency rooms, with the patient paying no more than in-network cost-sharing [S2][S3].

Lets women designate an OB-GYN as primary care provider and get routine gynecological and pregnancy care without a referral, and guarantees standing referrals and care coordination for chronic or life-threatening conditions [S2][S3].

Requires timely utilization-review decisions (within 3 business days for prior authorization, 1 day for continued care), bans compensation incentives tied to denying claims, and bars contract gag clauses that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options [S2][S3].
Requires internal and binding external appeals of coverage denials, with the plan paying the cost of the outside review [S2][S3].

Amends ERISA so patients can sue health plans and insurers in state court for damages from personal injury or wrongful death caused by denied care — closing the loophole that left most people with employer coverage no meaningful remedy [S2][S3].
Mandates at least 48 hours of hospital coverage after a mastectomy and coverage of reconstructive breast surgery, including symmetry procedures on the other breast [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans would bear the compliance costs: emergency and out-of-network coverage, network adequacy, quality data collection, external appeals (which they must pay for), and — the largest item — exposure to damage lawsuits under state law for denied care. Employers as plan sponsors would face some compliance costs too, though the bill largely shields them from lawsuits except when they directly decide a claim. Insurers would likely pass much of this to premiums paid by workers and employers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers with health plans

drawbacks.text: The bill stacks numerous coverage mandates and procedural requirements on every plan and issuer, and insurers and employer groups argued the compliance costs and new lawsuit exposure would raise premiums for everyone and push some employers to drop coverage altogether [S2][S3].

The right-to-sue provision opens plans and insurers to state-court damage awards for personal injury or wrongful death, which insurers said could drive up costs and defensive medicine; the bill does exempt employers from most such suits, confining liability to their direct benefit decisions [S2][S3].

The point-of-service option lets patients buy out-of-network coverage but explicitly allows plans to charge higher premiums and cost-sharing for it, and employers are not required to pay any of the added cost [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing denied or delayed care, the bill offered concrete, enforceable protections — especially the emergency-care guarantee, independent appeals, and a real right to sue that employer-based coverage lacked under ERISA. The costs are real but ordinary for any insurance regulation: higher administrative costs, some premium increases, and more litigation against plans. Whether the mandate-plus-lawsuit package was the right design was genuinely contested in 1998; critics preferred voluntary standards and external review without new liability. The bill is broadly drawn but not careless — it includes cost controls, employer liability limits, and plan-friendly carve-outs (for example, no new coverage mandate for drugs and devices).

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, then sent to three subcommittees, and none of them ever reported it out — so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 1998 on March 31, 1998, with House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt and about 100 other members as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It attracted 196 cosponsors in total — 185 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 10 Republicans — close to half the House [S4].
The Speaker sent it to the Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees simultaneously, each holding only the pieces within its jurisdiction [S1][S5].

In April and May 1998 it was referred to the Health, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations subcommittees; the record shows no hearings, no markup, and no floor action after that [S5].
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without any vote ever being taken on it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans were better off: no federal coverage mandates, no outside appeals they had to fund, and no state-court damage suits from denied-care claims. Patients in managed care got none of the protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 185 of 196 cosponsors, with 10 Republicans — and in the Republican-run House the bill never got a committee or floor vote; the 1998 patient-protection fight largely split along party lines.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill would force plans to cover out-of-network emergency care without pre-authorization, run independent appeals they must pay for, and face state-court damage suits for denied care — directly cutting into the utilization-review and claims-denial practices that managed care used to control costs. Its defeat left those practices and ERISA's shield against patient lawsuits intact.

Employers would take on compliance costs for plan rules, but the bill deliberately shields them from lawsuits except when they personally decide a benefits claim — a tradeoff meant to keep them from dropping coverage. Its failure spared them the compliance burden while preserving their workers' lack of legal remedies.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill bans gag clauses in plan contracts, prohibits compensation schemes that punish doctors for recommending care, protects doctors who report quality problems from retaliation, and guarantees standing referrals and network adequacy. Providers and their patients' interests ran together here.
